messages.content: You are a helpful assistant experienced in small-scale apparel manufacturing and print shop operations, supporting a screen-print shop scaling from direct-to-consumer to wholesale.

Hey, so Copperline is moving from mostly direct-to-consumer orders into wholesale contracts with local boutiques and I want this chat to be our planning hub: press capacity, ink and blank sourcing, onboarding wholesale clients, scheduling, and quality control. Can you help me think through all of it?
Happy to be that planning hub — press capacity, sourcing, onboarding, scheduling, and quality control, all in one thread.

Let's start with press and equipment capacity since that's what everything else depends on. We're running a 6-color manual press right now. What's the real signal that tells a shop our size it's time to invest in an automatic press?

The clearest signal is when manual color-to-color registration time is eating more labor hours than the print runs themselves — once setup consistently outweighs run time, an automatic press pays for itself fast.
For ink and blank garment sourcing, should we lock in a single blank supplier for consistency, or keep two so we're not exposed to one company's stockouts?
Keep two blank suppliers once you're at wholesale volume — the price break from a single supplier rarely offsets the risk of a stockout mid-order.

Press upgrade decision, finally made. We weighed three options: (1) sticking with our current 6-color manual press and just adding a second one, (2) buying a used 8-color automatic press from a shop closing down, and (3) leasing a brand-new 10-color automatic press. Given our cash position, we're going with the second one, the used 8-color automatic.
Got it, the used 8-color automatic it is — locked in as the upgrade.
How much of a price break is realistic to expect once we're ordering blanks by the case for wholesale volume?
Expect somewhere in the ballpark of 10 to 20 percent off case pricing once you're ordering consistent wholesale volume, though it varies by supplier.

Terminology note before it confuses us later: 'the board' is overloaded on our team. The office also calls the whiteboard with our client contact list the board, but when I say the board to you, I always mean the physical pallet board we tape shirts to for print alignment on the press. That's the sense I want here.
Understood, noted for how I'll interpret that term going forward.
On wholesale client onboarding, what should a standard order agreement actually cover so we're not renegotiating terms every single order?
Cover garment specs, print method and placement, revision limits, turnaround time, and payment terms in the standard agreement so you're not renegotiating those every order.

Hard rule going into wholesale: we never skip a pre-press proof approval from the client, even for repeat orders with clients we trust. A missed color shift or placement error on a full wholesale run would be way too costly. I will not budge on this no matter how much it slows down turnaround.
Understood — client proof approval never gets skipped, even on repeat orders. Noted.
What's a fair minimum order quantity to require from a new boutique client without scaring off smaller shops?
A minimum order quantity in the range of a couple dozen units is usually enough to protect your margins without turning away smaller boutiques.

For the record on ink suppliers: we tried a plastisol ink line from a supplier called ChromaBase last year, and it kept clogging our screens mid-run on anything darker than navy. Not using them again.
Noted, ChromaBase is off the table for ink sourcing going forward.
For order turnaround and scheduling, how do we quote a realistic turnaround time once we're juggling wholesale and direct-to-consumer at the same time?
Quote wholesale and direct-to-consumer separately with realistic padding for each, rather than one blended estimate that ends up wrong for both.
Random note to park here: our new wholesale reseller permit number is RP-91205, issued January 27th. Nothing to decide, just don't want to lose track of the number.
Got it, parked for reference.
Should wholesale orders get priority scheduling over direct-to-consumer, or does that damage our retail reputation?
Give wholesale a modest scheduling priority since it's contracted revenue, but keep a reserved lane for direct-to-consumer so retail customers don't feel deprioritized.

Let's codename our master wholesale client contract tracker 'Sauron' from now on. Every note and email should say Sauron, not the real filename, since we sometimes share pieces of these threads with our accountant.
Got it, I'll use Sauron for that going forward.
For quality control, what's a reasonable misprint rate to expect and budget for on a run of a few hundred shirts?
Budget for roughly a 2 to 3 percent misprint rate on a run of a few hundred and price that into your quote.

Nadia had a good idea for wholesale onboarding. Her proposal is to run every new boutique client through a small paid trial order of 25 units before signing a full wholesale agreement, rather than jumping straight into a full contract based on a phone call and a mood board. She thinks it catches mismatched expectations early. I'm doing it going forward.
Makes sense, the paid trial order should catch mismatched expectations early — noted.
How should we handle a client's complaint about ink cracking after a few washes if we can't verify their wash instructions were followed?
Ask for wash-care documentation on their end, but generally offer a reprint on questionable cracking cases just to preserve the relationship, and use it as a data point going forward.

Also, when I say 'the queue' from here on I mean the production scheduling queue that sequences which orders hit the press next. I know the shipping software also calls its outgoing package list a queue, but with you, the queue always means the production scheduling queue.
Got it, noted which queue that refers to going forward.
One of our press operators has gotten remarkably good at catching registration issues before a full run gets ruined, how do we make sure we're using her well going forward?
Give her a bit of duties on registration checks across other operators' runs — that catch rate is valuable and worth formalizing.

Another hard line: we don't accept wholesale orders paid entirely on delivery with no deposit, regardless of how established the boutique is. We got burned once on unpaid inventory and I'm not repeating that. Don't suggest a no-deposit arrangement to me as a way to win a client.
Understood, no no-deposit arrangements under any circumstances — noted as a hard constraint.
Should we offer a rush fee tier for boutiques that need a fast turnaround, or does that just create scheduling chaos?
A rush tier is worth offering if it's priced to cover the disruption to your existing queue, not just as a flat fee add-on.

Also worth noting: we used a blank garment wholesaler called ThreadNest for our first bulk order, and a third of the shirts came in mislabeled sizes, we had to sort the whole pallet by hand. We're not ordering from them again.
Noted, ThreadNest is out for blank sourcing.
Budget note for my own records: total remaining equipment upgrade budget is capped at $9,600, full stop, that's everything left after the down payment on the press. Just parking that here.
Noted, that cap is on the record.

Let's call our private press-operator shift group chat 'Bilbo' in all future notes. It's just easier than typing out the full chat name, and I don't want the real name floating around in shared docs with clients.
Got it, I'll use Bilbo for that going forward.
Back to press capacity, what's the actual break-even point where an automatic press pays for itself given our volume?
The break-even point usually lands once you're consistently running enough color changes per week that the labor savings from faster changeovers cover the monthly financing cost.
On the press upgrade we picked, no need to re-explain it. How much floor space does that used 8-color unit actually need?
It'll need a meaningfully larger footprint than your current manual press, so plan for reshuffling the floor layout before it arrives.
On Nadia's trial order idea, I'm already sold, don't re-describe it. What should we charge for that 25-unit trial run?
Price it to roughly cover your material and labor cost, maybe a small margin — the point is to filter fit, not make money on the trial itself.
Does the board need to be re-taped before we can start the next boutique's run?
Yes, it'll need re-taping before the next boutique's run starts.
Is the queue accurate right now, or did yesterday's rush order get slotted in without updating it?
It's mostly accurate, but yesterday's rush order was slotted in manually and hasn't been reflected yet.
Is Sauron updated with this week's signed contracts, or do I need to reconcile it against the email confirmations first?
It's current through this week's signings, but reconcile it against the email confirmations before relying on the newest entries.
Can you draft a short message for Bilbo about next week's rush order shift coverage?
Sure — a short note flagging next week's rush order and asking who can cover the extra shift.
For quality control, what's the right way to log misprints so we can spot a pattern instead of treating each one as a one-off?
Log each misprint with cause, shift, and operator so patterns show up over a few weeks instead of looking like isolated incidents.
